thread.title: What Facebook's Show With Cristiano Ronaldo Might Tell Us About The Future - Facebook (NASDAQ:FB) | Seeking Alpha

author: Nicholas Ward
title: What Facebook's Show With Cristiano Ronaldo Might Tell Us About The Future - Facebook (NASDAQ:FB) | Seeking Alpha
text:
Video content is all the rage right now. AT&T ( T ) just paid a handsome fee to add video content to its distribution pipes with its acquisition of Time Warner ( TWX ). This recent article in the Economist projects that Netflix ( NFLX ) will spend roughly $12-13b on content in 2018, more than any other content studio. With its ~80 feature film slate for 2018, some argue that Netflix is simply throwing expensive spaghetti at the wall, hoping that some of it sticks and turns into big hits. Either way, ~$12.5b is much less than the ~$85b that AT&T paid for Time Warner, so maybe NFLX has it right. Disney ( DIS ) is looking to spend billions and billions on Fox ( FOX ). Comcast ( CMCSA ) has thrown its hat in that ring as well. YouTube has grown into one of the most watched content sources in the world. Apple ( AAPL ) recently entered into a multi-year relationship with Oprah Winfrey . Social media platforms across the gambit have taken strides towards increasing their video loads. Advertisers pay much more to be associated with video content. With all of this in mind, it comes as no surprise to me that Facebook ( FB ) is making a big splash with the announcement that it's in talks for an upcoming reality series centered around Cristiano Ronaldo, who is arguably the most popular athlete in the entire world.
There are two ways to look at this video-centric phenomena. First of all, it’s well known that Hollywood studios have been a good place for rich people to lose money for decades. Making movies is very hit and miss and we’ve entered into a world where just a few blockbusters each year are taking in the vast majority of the box office proceeds. I could see a scenario where all of this content spending is emblematic of late cycle euphoria.
However, I could also imagine a world where virtual reality essentially replaces actual reality and content producers will be in higher demand than ever before. I think we’re a long way off from that sort of reality, but I know that the world is becoming more and more efficient and billions of individuals are looking for a way to spend their free time. Screens are becoming more mobile, affordable, and widespread. Boredom is becoming a thing of the past.
As hardware is commoditized, companies are looking for to bolster their bottom lines with high margin services. Once you’ve developed a massive user base, adding video content and monetizing it either via advertisements or even better, reoccurring paid subscriptions, is a relatively easy decision to make.
What’s more, adding content to an existing network works as a two-way street. Not only does the content potentially generate added income and diversify a company’s revenue stream, but it increases the value that the content has to the consumer in the first place, making that ecosystem even stickier long-term.
Facebook’s family of networks (Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, etc) are viewed by billions of people on a daily basis. There isn’t a television network in the world than can compete with this viewership. Even Netflix can’t compete with this (Netflix has ~$125 million subscribers).
Now, FB is a free platform, which explains its broad engagement. It’s no easy feat to convince someone to pay for something that they’ve become accustomed to for free. With that said, in an increasing globalized world with privacy issues abound, I can imagine a day when FB offers a premium subscription. The thing is, I don’t think people are going to be willing to pay purely for privacy. Facebook has to sweeten the pot a bit. One way to do so is to draw users in with original content.
I have to admit, that this is all purely speculative. During his Congressional hearings, Mark Zuckerberg did seem to be open to the idea of a premium segment of his network though. This played a role in my decision to re-purchase the FB shares that I sold during the Cambridge Analytica scandal.
I haven’t heard word of any plans to introduce such a plan for interested users since. I imagine that FB is trying not to rock the boat at all right now with investigations ongoing. However, in the event that management ever does announce a paid option, I imagine the stock’s price will sky rocket. Even if only a small percentage of FB’s user base signs up for a premium service, we’re still talking about a very large sum of money essentially dropping to the company’s bottom-line.
And where better to start drawing attention to your video platform than with the most popular player in the most popular sport during the most popular sporting event in the world? As an American I realize I cannot truly appreciate the popularity of Ronaldo, but statistics don’t lie. Ronaldo has nearly ~121m followers of Facebook, 74.3m followers on Twitter, and 133m followers on Instagram.
For comparison, LeBron James has ~23m followers of Facebook, 41.9m on Twitter, and 39.2m on Instagram. Tom Brady only has 4.3m followers of Facebook and 4.2m of Instagram (as far as I know, Mr. Brady doesn’t have a twitter; this doesn’t surprise me, being a member of the Patriots and all).
Heck, Ronaldo even has a bigger social media presence than Donald Trump, the POTUS, leader of the free world, who’s sometimes (affectionately) referred to as President-in-Tweet. Donald J. Trump has 24.6m Facebook followers, 53.2m followers on Twitter, and 9.2m followers on Instagram. If that doesn’t paint a fairly clear picture of just how big of a superstar Cristiano Ronaldo is, I don’t know what will.
Partnering with Ronaldo seems like a great idea for Facebook. What’s even better is that the reports say that the deal is only going to cost FB ~$10m to partner with Ronaldo. $10m is just a drop in the bucket for the soccer superstar. We're talking about a man that makes $100m+ annually and has a lifetime contract with Nike ( NKE ) that is reported to be " worth upwards of $1 billion. " I’m surprised he was willing to work for that relatively small amount; however, I think this sheds a light on the reality of the situation for superstars and a Facebook partnership…this too, is a two-way street.
Both entities in this partnership are growing their respective brands alongside one another. This is an added benefit that social media platforms can give stars/content creators when selling their pitch. I’ve always thought that Twitter ( TWTR ) really missed out on getting into live broadcasts because of the potential synergies of the social watching experience (so often, we’re all on social media, making posts and commenting on others’ during major events, especially those of the sporting variety). If Facebook is able to get rid of the middleman (a login and a few clicks), putting attractive/original content on a socially interactive screen, I think that’s the next obvious evolution of the social media experience.
If Facebook’s algorithms can prove that partnering with them directly for content boosts social engagements/likes/follows/money coming in from digital advertisers, I think it’s possible that this competitive advantage over non-social distribution platforms will provide them with discounts in terms of content creation. In a world where influences pay for followers, likes, etc, Facebook could essentially use bits and pieces of its social sphere as commodities. Or, at the very least, as incentives as a part of a deal.
What’s more, Facebook already has the cash flows coming in from its digital advertisement business to fund the content creation (discounted or not). I like FB’s targeted approach (partnering with a superstar like Ronaldo, rather than the spaghetti-esque approach that Netflix is taking). Fundamentally, it isn’t dealing with the same stigma that Netflix has regarding cash burn and a lack of profits. This is obviously just the beginning, but I wouldn’t be totally surprised if in 5-10 years, Facebook has drawn even with Netflix and others in the video distribution space. Furthermore, I think FB could do it with significantly less invested capital.
I understand that’s a pretty bold statement and I’m sure that many will refute it, but I’m happy to hold onto my shares and wait and see. Thankfully, they’re priced fairly attractively on a fundamental basis (using forward growth estimates), so I’m not taking a huge speculative risk one way or the other.
Disclosure: I am/we are long FB, DIS, CMCSA, AAPL, T.
I wrote this article myself, and it expresses my own opinions. I am not for it (other than from Seeking Alpha). I have no business relationship with any company whose stock is mentioned in this article.
